title: Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau
wiki_lead:
Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau (German: [ˌdiːtʁɪç ˌfɪʃɐ ˈdiːskaʊ̯] ; 28 May 1925 – 18 May 2012) was a German lyric baritone and conductor of classical music. One of the most famous Lieder (art song) performers of the post-war period, he is best known as a singer of Franz Schubert's Lieder, particularly "Winterreise" of which his recordings with accompanists Gerald Moore and Jörg Demus are still critically acclaimed half a century after their release.
Because he recorded an array of repertoire (spanning centuries), musicologist Alan Blyth asserted, "No singer in our time, or probably any other has managed the range and versatility of repertory achieved by Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau. Opera, Lieder and oratorio in German, Italian or English came alike to him, yet he brought to each a precision and individuality that bespoke his perceptive insights into the idiom at hand." In addition, he recorded in French, Russian, Hebrew, Latin and Hungarian. He was described as "one of the supreme vocal artists of the 20th century" and "the most influential singer of the 20th Century".
Fischer-Dieskau was ranked the second greatest singer of the century (after Jussi Björling) by Classic CD (United Kingdom) "Top Singers of the Century" Critics' Poll (June 1999). The French dubbed him "Le miracle Fischer-Dieskau" and Dame Elisabeth Schwarzkopf called him "a born god who has it all." At his peak, he was greatly admired for his interpretive insights and exceptional control of his soft, beautiful voice. He dominated both the opera and concert platforms for over thirty years.

Life and career
Albert Dietrich Fischer was born in 1925 in Berlin to Albert Fischer, a school principal, and Theodora (née Klingelhoffer) Fischer, a teacher. In 1934, his father added the hyphenated "Dieskau" to the family name (through his mother, he was descended from the Kammerherr von Dieskau, for whom Johann Sebastian Bach wrote the "Peasant Cantata"). He started singing as a child and began formal voice lessons at the age of 16. When he was drafted into the Wehrmacht during World War II in 1943, tending horses on the Russian Front, Fischer-Dieskau had just completed his secondary school studies and one semester at the Berlin Conservatory. He served in Grenadier Regiment 146 of the 65th Infantry Division south of Bologna in the winter of 1944–45 and entertained his comrades at soldiers' evenings behind the lines.
He was captured in Italy in 1945 and spent two years as an American prisoner of war. During that time, he sang Lieder in POW camps to homesick German soldiers. He had a physically and intellectually impaired brother, Martin, who was sent to an institution by the Nazi regime and starved to death. Their family home was destroyed during the war.


Singing career
In 1947, Fischer-Dieskau returned to Germany, where he launched his professional career as a singer in Badenweiler, singing in Brahms's Ein Deutsches Requiem without any rehearsal. (He was a last-minute substitute for an indisposed singer.) He gave his first Lieder recital in Leipzig in late 1947 and followed it soon afterwards with a highly successful first concert at Berlin's Titania-Palast.
From early in his career he collaborated with famous lyric sopranos Elisabeth Schwarzkopf and Irmgard Seefried, and the recording producer Walter Legge, issuing instantly successful albums of Lieder by Schubert and Hugo Wolf.
In late 1948, Fischer-Dieskau was engaged as principal lyric baritone at the Städtische Oper Berlin (Municipal Opera, West Berlin), making his debut as Posa in Verdi's Don Carlos under Ferenc Fricsay. This company, known after 1961 as the Deutsche Oper, would remain his artistic home until his retirement from the operatic stage, in 1978.

grok_lead: Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau (28 May 1925 â 18 May 2012) was a German baritone opera singer, conductor, and vocal pedagogue, widely acclaimed as one of the 20th century's greatest interpreters of German lieder and a pioneering figure in vocal music recording. Born in Berlin to academic parents, he began singing as a child and started formal vocal studies at age 16 with Georg Walter and Hermann Weissenborn. Drafted into the Wehrmacht in 1943 during World War II, he was captured by Allied forces in Italy in 1945 and repatriated in 1947, after which he quickly rose to prominence by substituting in a performance of Brahms's German Requiem. Fischer-Dieskau made his operatic debut in 1948 as the Marquis of Posa in Verdi's Don Carlos at the Berlin City Opera, launching a career that spanned major venues including the Vienna State Opera, Bavarian State Opera, Bayreuth Festival (1954â1956), and Covent Garden (debut 1965 as Mandryka in Strauss's Arabella). He excelled in a wide repertoire of over 100 operatic roles, including Kurwenal in Wagner's Tristan und Isolde (recorded 1952), Papageno in Mozart's Die ZauberflÃ¶te, and Falstaff in Verdi's opera (final concert performance 1992 in Munich), having retired from the staged opera repertoire in 1978 to focus on lieder. His lieder performances, particularly of works by Schubert, Schumann, Brahms, Wolf, Mahler, and Strauss, set new standards for interpretive depth and lyrical expression, with collaborations alongside pianist Gerald Moore defining the genre for generations. He recorded the complete songs of these composers, including eight versions of Schubert's Winterreise âhis first public recital of it in 1943âand championed contemporary pieces like Britten's War Requiem (for which the baritone solo was written) and Samuel Barber's 3 Songs, Op. 45. With hundreds of recordings, Fischer-Dieskau became the most prolific vocal artist in history, earning five Grammy Awards and 25 nominations, including wins in 1971 for Schubert lieder and 1973 for Brahms's SchÃ¶ne Magelone. Notable releases include Mahler's Das Lied von der Erde with conductors like Paul Kletzki and Leonard Bernstein, and live Salzburg Festival performances such as Le nozze di Figaro (1962). After retiring from singing in 1992 following final recitals in Berlin and London, he continued as a conductor, reciter of literary texts, and influential teacher starting in 1983, mentoring singers like JÃºlia VÃ¡rady (his fourth wife since 1977) and Benjamin Appl. He also authored memoirs such as Echoes of a Lifetime (1989) and a biography of Johann Friedrich Reichardt, reflecting his scholarly approach to music. Fischer-Dieskau's legacy endures as a transformative force in vocal music, praised for his honeyed tone, technical mastery, and ability to convey profound emotional nuance, inspiring countless performers and expanding the audience for lieder worldwide; his 100th birthday in 2025 was marked by numerous commemorative events and publications.
